method: Questions were researched with an evidence-only retrieval tool over one corpus of open-access and public-domain texts (see corpus.json). Each excerpt was checked word for word against the corpus passage it cites when this file was written; corpus_chunk numbers that passage in the corpus snapshot of 2026-10-01.
questions: How did classical Chinese thinkers understand knowledge?
What are the Mohist three standards (fa), and how are they justified?
How should Zhuangzi's butterfly dream be read?
What did Xunzi say about the heart-mind and blindness?

evidence.excerpt: (or primarily) stems from moral training
epistemology is inseparable from ontology
The three fa are that statements must have a root, a source, and a use.
The “source” is that statements must have an empirical basis; they must be checked against what people see and hear.
the statement must produce benefit
The “root” is the historical precedent and evidence provided by the deeds of the ancient sage kings
the Mohists seem to overlook the possibility of conflicts between the three, such as the likelihood that certain practices of the ancient sage-kings might not benefit society today
The texts that present the theory do not say, but the Mohists probably view the third standard, benefit to society, as an application of their moral theory
Concerns can be raised about the vagueness of the three standards
the extent to which the Mohists apply them fairly and rigorously
dreamt of being a butterfly or a butterfly is dreaming of being Zhuangzi—though there must be a difference. This is called “things change”.
The mild skepticism of our trajectory to greater knowledge is most famously illustrated in the story of Zhuangzi dreaming being a butterfly
Zhuangzi’s relativism is mildly skeptical of the relativism itself.
